title: Parliament

cards.b:
Parliament is the centre of the parliamentary system. It makes laws, controls money and holds the executive to account. Yet scholars and presiding officers have warned for years that its working is declining: fewer sittings, frequent disruptions, less committee scrutiny.

UPSC asks about structure and powers, the role of the Rajya Sabha, the committee system, the Speaker and the decline of Parliament. You need articles, numbers, examples and a view.

Walter Bagehot, in The English Constitution (1867), listed five functions of the House of Commons: the elective function (choosing the government), the expressive (voicing the people's mind), the teaching, the informing and the legislative. Many add scrutiny of the executive as the most important today.

cards.h: Structure: President, Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha
cards.b:
Lok Sabha (Articles 81-83)

Maximum 550 members (530 from states, 20 from Union Territories). Present strength is 543; the 104th Amendment (2019) ended the two nominated Anglo-Indian seats. Five-year term, which can be extended one year at a time during a national Emergency. Minimum age 25. Led by the Speaker (Article 93).

Rajya Sabha (Articles 80, 83)

Maximum 250: 238 from states and Union Territories, and 12 nominated for expertise in literature, science, art or social service. Present strength is 245. A permanent House: one-third retire every two years; six-year term. Minimum age 30. Chaired by the Vice-President.

Rajya Sabha members are elected indirectly by state assemblies using the single transferable vote. Seats are allotted by population, not equally as in the US Senate. The domicile requirement was removed in 2003, and open ballot was introduced for the Rajya Sabha elections.

The Lok Sabha has the last word on money bills, the control over the Council of Ministers, and in joint sittings (the Lok Sabha has more members).

cards.h: How a bill becomes a law
cards.b:
• Ordinary bill: either House, equal powers. The Rajya Sabha may delay but not block a money bill.
  • Money bill (Article 110): only in the Lok Sabha, on the President's recommendation. The Rajya Sabha can only recommend changes within 14 days; the Lok Sabha may reject them. The Speaker certifies a bill as a money bill.
  • Constitutional amendment: both Houses by special majority; no joint sitting.
  • Joint sitting has been used three times: Dowry Prohibition Bill (1961), Banking Service Commission Repeal Bill (1978), Prevention of Terrorism Bill (2002).

• Article 112: the annual financial statement. Presented on 1 February since 2017, when the Railway Budget was merged with the Union Budget.
  • The government cannot spend from the Consolidated Fund (Article 266) without Parliament's authorisation through an Appropriation Act. A Contingency Fund (Article 267) is for unforeseen needs.
  • Stages: general discussion; demands for grants (cut motions are used to signal protest); the Appropriation Bill; the Finance Bill. A guillotine ends debate on remaining demands.
  • Control after spending: the CAG audits; the Public Accounts Committee examines the reports.

Controversy: the Aadhaar Act, 2016 was passed as a money bill, which kept the Rajya Sabha out. In K.S. Puttaswamy (Aadhaar) (2018), a 4:1 majority upheld this. In Rojer Mathew (2019), the Court referred the wider question of misuse of the money bill route to a larger bench. The issue is still pending.

• Question Hour (starred, unstarred, short notice), Zero Hour (an Indian invention, since 1962), and calling-attention notices.
  • Motions: adjournment motion, no-confidence motion (under Rule 198, needs 50 members to support), censure, cut motions and motion of thanks to the President's address.
  • Debates: short-duration discussions, half-hour discussions.
  • Committees: the main arm of scrutiny.

Main committees

Public Accounts Committee (since 1921; the Chair is traditionally from the Opposition), Estimates Committee (1950), Committee on Public Undertakings (1964), and Department-Related Standing Committees (set up in 1993, now 24). Joint Parliamentary Committees are ad hoc: examples are the Bofors (1987), the stock market scam (1992), the 2G (2011) and the 2025 Waqf bill committee.

• The Speaker is elected by the Lok Sabha (Article 93) and presides, decides on points of order, certifies money bills, decides on defections under the Tenth Schedule and disqualification, and has a casting vote only in a tie.
  • G.V. Mavalankar, the first Speaker (1952-56), set conventions of impartiality. Neelam Sanjiva Reddy resigned from his party on becoming Speaker (1967).
  • The Speaker does not vacate the seat on dissolution but remains till the new House meets.
  • Deputy Speaker: traditionally from the Opposition; the post stayed vacant throughout the 17th Lok Sabha (2019-24).
  • Speaker Om Birla was re-elected in the 18th Lok Sabha on 26 June 2024. The Leader of the Opposition, Rahul Gandhi, was recognised after a gap of ten years.

Criticism: Speakers belong to parties, so their decisions on defection and suspension often seem partisan. The Supreme Court (Kihoto Hollohan, 1992; Keisham Meghachandra Singh, 2020) has asked for timely and reviewable decisions.

Strengths: it represents states and, in theory, offers a second look at bills; it protects continuity (it cannot be dissolved); it brings in experts through nominated members; it has special federal powers: Article 249 (Parliament can legislate on State List subjects if two-thirds of the Rajya Sabha agrees in the national interest), Article 312 (creating All India Services).

Weaknesses:

  • Seats go by population, so it is not an equal federal chamber like the US Senate.
  • It has been used by parties to place leaders who cannot win elections. The residence rule was removed in 2003.
  • It has less power than the Lok Sabha on money and in confidence votes.

The Sarkaria Commission and the NCRWC (2002) saw it as useful but wanted it more representative of states. Still, it has delayed or amended important bills, such as the Lokpal Bill (2011-13).

• Sittings: the first Lok Sabha sat for about 135 days a year (an average above 120 in the 1950s). Recent Houses sit for roughly 55-70 days a year (PRS Legislative Research).
  • Disruptions: repeated walkouts and adjournments waste time. In December 2023, 146 MPs were suspended in the winter session. Bills passed in disrupted sessions get less debate.
  • Committee scrutiny: the share of bills sent to committees fell from 71% in the 15th Lok Sabha to about 16% in the 17th (PRS).
  • Ordinances and money bills are used to bypass the Rajya Sabha.
  • Anti-defection law reduces MPs' independence, since party whips rule.

Reforms suggested: a minimum number of sitting days (the National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution suggested 120 for the Lok Sabha and 100 for the Rajya Sabha), automatic referral of bills to committees, a Parliamentary Budget Office, Opposition-chaired committees and a less partisan Speaker.

• After the 2024 election, the BJP-led NDA has 293 members, and the INDIA bloc 234, giving a stronger Opposition than the 17th Lok Sabha.
  • Waqf (Amendment) Bill, 2024-25: sent to a Joint Parliamentary Committee of 31 members before passage in April 2025.
  • Three new criminal laws (Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita and others) took effect on 1 July 2024.
  • Constitutional bills: the 129th Amendment (simultaneous elections) and 130th (removal of ministers in custody) are with JPCs. The 131st Amendment Bill failed on 17 April 2026 for want of a two-thirds majority.
  • New Parliament building (inaugurated 28 May 2023) and the women's reservation law (106th Amendment, notified 16 April 2026) are changes in form and composition.
  • Debates on the SIR of electoral rolls and on foreign policy episodes tested whether the Opposition can force discussion.

"Parliament's role as a legislature has diminished. Discuss the reasons and remedies."
"Examine the role of parliamentary committees in strengthening accountability."
"Does the Rajya Sabha serve any useful purpose?"
"The Speaker's role has become controversial. Examine."

Structure: Bagehot's functions; composition and powers; law-making and money bills; budget control; committees; Speaker and Rajya Sabha; indicators of decline (sittings, committees, disruptions); reforms (NCRWC 120 days, committees); recent cases (Waqf JPC, 2023 suspensions); end with a hopeful view.
